vignette:
Margaret is a 57-year-old pastoral care worker who still remembers the exact sound-a screech of tires, then the sickening crunch of metal folding into metal. That January evening two years ago, she was riding in the passenger seat of a colleague's car on their way to visit a homebound parishioner. A pickup truck ran a red light and slammed into the driver's side door. The impact spun the car twice before it came to rest against a utility pole. Margaret was pinned for nearly twenty minutes, her legs numb, her chest pressed against the seatbelt so hard she could barely draw breath. She could hear her colleague moaning in the driver's seat, but she could not move, could not do anything, could only wait for help that seemed to take forever to arrive. When the paramedics finally cut her out, she vomited from the adrenaline and the pain. In the emergency room, a doctor told her she was lucky-only a cracked rib and deep bruising. Margaret did not feel lucky. She felt hollowed out, violated by the sheer randomness of the event. The other driver received a minor speeding ticket. No charges, no apology, nothing.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret tried to resume her normal routines. She needed to drive to visit families, to attend meetings at the community center, to check on elderly members of her congregation. But every time she got behind the wheel of her own car, her hands began to shake and her heart pounded so hard she thought she might pass out. Being a passenger was worse-she could not brace herself, could not control the speed, could not see the intersections before it was too late. Within a month, she had stopped driving altogether. She began walking to work, a forty-minute commute that left her exhausted, or taking the bus, which had its own terrors: she always sat near the rear exit door, scanning the road ahead for any vehicle that might veer into their lane. Even the gentle thump of a bus over a pothole made her flinch. What she had not anticipated was how the bus could trap her. One afternoon, the bus became crowded and she was forced to stand in the center aisle, pinned between other passengers, unable to move toward the exit. Her chest tightened, her vision blurred-she was certain she would faint or vomit, just as she had when the paramedics cut her free. She began to dread any situation where she could not leave on her own terms: standing in a checkout line, sitting in a windowless office, even waiting for a slow microwave to finish. The feeling of being compelled to stay, to endure, was unbearable.

Margaret discovered that stillness itself had become unbearable. When she came home from work, she would pace the floor of her small apartment rather than sit down. On Sunday afternoons, when she used to read or nap, she now found herself cleaning the kitchen or reorganizing her closets. The moment she allowed herself to let go, to relax, a wave of fear washed over her-a certainty that something terrible was waiting for her in that quiet space. She began to believe that vigilance was the only thing keeping her safe. If she stayed alert, if she never let her guard down, maybe she could outrun the next disaster. But her body gave her constant reminders that it could not be trusted. Walking too fast up the stairs made her heart race, and she would stop, dizzy and frightened, convinced she was about to faint or collapse. She gave up the evening jogs she had loved for years. Physical exertion felt like a betrayal, a pressure that her fragile body could not withstand.

At the community center where she worked, Margaret started to notice details she had never seen before. The location of every fire extinguisher, every emergency exit, every door that was locked versus unlocked. She would slip out of staff meetings if the room had only one entrance, claiming she needed water or a phone call. When a coworker tried to comfort her, saying, "You're safe here, Margaret, the doors are always locked," Margaret did not believe them. It was impossible to believe. Safety had been a lie her whole life; she knew now that safety could be shattered in an instant by a stranger who ran a red light. She began to avoid the weekly home visits that were central to her job, offering to do phone check-ins instead. Her supervisor noticed, gently asked if she needed time off. Margaret said no. She was terrified that if she admitted how bad it was, she would lose her job, and then she would truly have nothing.

What haunted her most was the sense that the accident had been profoundly unfair, and that no one had acknowledged it. She had been a passenger, an innocent woman on her way to help someone else, and she had been broken for no reason. The thought circled in her mind: This should not have happened, and nothing has been done to make it right. She came to believe that if the world could treat her that way once, then it could do so again at any moment. She had no power to stop it. She could not trust her own body to be strong, could not trust other drivers to be careful, could not trust buildings to be safe. Her life had shrunk into a narrow corridor of routines designed to minimize risk, and even those routines felt fragile. At 57, she had always imagined her later years as a time of calm and purpose, but instead she felt stuck in a constant state of alert, waiting for the next moment when she would be forced to endure something beyond her control.

Margaret finally made an appointment with a therapist after a trigger she could not ignore: she was walking to work and heard a car backfire, and she dropped to her knees on the sidewalk, sobbing, unable to explain to the strangers who stared. That night, she knew she could not live this way any longer. She is afraid of what the therapy will ask her to do-to get back in a car, to sit still in a room without scanning the walls, to believe that her body will not betray her. But more than that, she is afraid of spending the rest of her life waiting for the next disaster to find her. She hopes, against reason, that someone might tell her that the world is not as dangerous as it now seems, and that she might one day believe them.
